subject: math
title: Adding and Subtracting to 20
seo_title: Grade 1 Adding and Subtracting to 20 Worksheets with Answer Key (Ontario)
standard_text: Use mental math strategies, including estimation, to add and subtract whole numbers that add up to no more than 20, and explain the strategies used
meta_desc: Free Grade 1 math worksheets on adding and subtracting to 20: doubles, near doubles, make ten, counting on and back on a number line, and thinking addition to subtract. 100 questions with pictures and an answer key, following the Ontario curriculum.
key_big: Use a strategy, not just your fingers: doubles, make ten, count on, or think addition.
key_sub: 6 + 7 is double 6 and 1 more: 13. 8 + 5 = 8 + 2 + 3 = 13. For 13 − 5, think 5 + 8 = 13.
body_html:
Doubles and near doubles

A double adds a number to itself. 6 + 6 = 12. 8 + 8 = 16.

A near double uses two numbers that are 1 apart. Use the double. Then add 1.

Make ten

Learn the pairs that make 10. To add past 10, make a 10 first. Then add the rest.

Makes 10Turn-around
1 + 99 + 1
2 + 88 + 2
3 + 77 + 3
4 + 66 + 4
5 + 55 + 5
Example

What is 9 + 4?

9 + 1 = 10. 3 are left. 10 + 3 = 13.

Answer: 13

Count on and count back

To add a small number, start at the big number and count on. To take away a small number, count back. Count the jumps, not the start number.

Example

What is 13 − 2?

Start at 13. Count back 2: 12, 11.

Answer: 11

Think addition to subtract

Adding and taking away go together. If you know 8 + 5 = 13, you know 13 − 5 = 8 and 13 − 8 = 5.

Example

What is 12 − 9?

Think: 9 + ? = 12. Count up: 10, 11, 12. That is 3.

Answer: 3

Check a subtraction with an addition. 12 − 9 = 3, and 3 + 9 = 12. It checks.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
8 + 3 = 10 (saying 8, 9, 10)Do not say the start number. Say 9, 10, 11. So 8 + 3 = 11.
13 − 5 = 12 (doing 5 − 3)You cannot take 5 from 3. Think: 5 + 8 = 13. So 13 − 5 = 8.
7 + 8 = 147 + 7 = 14. 8 is 1 more, so 7 + 8 = 15.
2 + 9: counting on 9 from 2Start with the bigger number. 9, then 10, 11. So 2 + 9 = 11.

faq.q: What does Grade 1 math in Ontario expect for adding and subtracting?
faq.a: The Ontario Mathematics Curriculum (2020) asks Grade 1 students to use mental math strategies to add and subtract whole numbers that add up to no more than 20, and to explain the strategy they used.

faq.q: What are mental math strategies for adding to 20?
faq.a: Common Grade 1 strategies are doubles (6 + 6), near doubles (6 + 7 is double 6 and 1 more), making ten (8 + 5 = 8 + 2 + 3), and counting on from the bigger number.

faq.q: Why does my child get answers that are 1 off when counting on?
faq.a: They are usually saying the start number as the first count, like “8, 9, 10” for 8 + 3. Have them hold the 8 in their head and count the jumps: 9, 10, 11.

faq.q: How can I help my child subtract at home?
faq.a: Link each subtraction to an addition fact. For 13 − 5, ask “5 plus what makes 13?” A ten frame drawn on paper and some coins or buttons make it easy to see.

items.q: Each frame has 2 counters. What is 2 + 2?
items.e: Both frames have 2. This is a double. 2 + 2 = 4.

items.q: Each frame has 3 counters. What is 3 + 3?
items.e: Both frames have 3. This is a double. 3 + 3 = 6.

items.q: Each frame has 5 counters. What is 5 + 5?
items.e: Both frames have 5. This is a double. 5 + 5 = 10.

items.q: Each frame has 6 counters. What is 6 + 6?
items.e: Both frames have 6. This is a double. 6 + 6 = 12.

items.q: Each frame has 9 counters. What is 9 + 9?
items.e: Both frames have 9. This is a double. 9 + 9 = 18.

items.q: Each frame has 10 counters. What is 10 + 10?
items.e: Both frames have 10. This is a double. 10 + 10 = 20.

items.q: Each row has 4 apples. What is double 4?
items.e: Double 4 means 4 + 4. 4 + 4 = 8.

items.q: Each row has 7 apples. What is double 7?
items.e: Double 7 means 7 + 7. 7 + 7 = 14.

items.q: Each row has 8 apples. What is double 8?
items.e: Double 8 means 8 + 8. 8 + 8 = 16.

items.q: Use double 4. What is 4 + 5?
items.e: Double 4 is 8. The blue counter is 1 more. 8 + 1 = 9.

items.q: Use double 5. What is 5 + 6?
items.e: Double 5 is 10. The blue counter is 1 more. 10 + 1 = 11.

items.q: Use double 6. What is 6 + 7?
items.e: Double 6 is 12. The blue counter is 1 more. 12 + 1 = 13.

items.q: Use double 8. What is 8 + 9?
items.e: Double 8 is 16. The blue counter is 1 more. 16 + 1 = 17.

items.q: What is 8 + 7?
items.e: Double 7 is 14. 8 is 1 more than 7. 14 + 1 = 15.

items.q: Which one is a double?
items.e: A double adds a number to itself. 6 + 6 is a double.

items.q: Which one is a near double?
items.e: A near double uses two numbers that are 1 apart. 5 and 6 are 1 apart. So 5 + 6 is a near double.

items.q: Double what number makes 14?
items.e: 7 + 7 = 14. So double 7 makes 14. (14 is the total.)

items.q: Owen says 6 + 7 = 12. What did he forget?
items.e: 6 + 6 = 12. But 7 is 1 more than 6. So 6 + 7 = 12 + 1 = 13. Owen forgot to add 1.

items.q: Double 6 is 12. What is 12 − 6?
items.e: 6 + 6 = 12. So 12 − 6 = 6. (18 adds instead of taking away.)

items.q: Double 8 is 16. What is 16 − 8?
items.e: 8 + 8 = 16. So 16 − 8 = 8. (24 adds instead of taking away.)

items.q: How many more counters make 10?
items.e: There are 3 empty spaces. 7 + 3 = 10. So 3 more make 10.

items.q: How many more counters make 10?
items.e: There are 6 empty spaces. 4 + 6 = 10. So 6 more make 10.

items.q: How many more counters make 10?
items.e: There is 1 empty space. 9 + 1 = 10. So 1 more makes 10.

items.q: How many more counters make 10?
items.e: There are 4 empty spaces. 6 + 4 = 10. So 4 more make 10.

items.q: What goes with 2 to make 10?
items.e: 2 + 8 = 10. So the number is 8. (12 adds 10 to 2.)

items.q: Which pair makes 10?
Which pair does NOT make 10?
items.e: 3 + 6 = 9, not 10. So 3 + 6 does not make 10.

items.q: One frame is full. What is 10 + 6?
items.e: A full frame is 10. 10 and 6 more is 16.

items.q: Fill the top frame first. What is 9 + 3?
Fill the top frame first. What is 8 + 5?
Fill the top frame first. What is 9 + 6?
Fill the top frame first. What is 7 + 4?
Fill the top frame first. What is 8 + 6?
8 + 5 = 8 + 2 + ?. What is the missing number?
items.e: 8 + 2 makes 10. Split the 5 into 2 and 3. So 8 + 5 = 10 + 3 = 13.

items.q: 9 + 4 = 9 + 1 + ?. What is the missing number?
items.e: 9 + 1 makes 10. Split the 4 into 1 and 3. So 9 + 4 = 10 + 3 = 13.

items.q: 9 + 7 = 9 + 1 + ?. What is the missing number?
items.e: 9 + 1 makes 10. Split the 7 into 1 and 6. So 9 + 7 = 10 + 6 = 16.

items.q: 7 + 5 = 7 + 3 + ?. What is the missing number?
items.e: 7 + 3 makes 10. Split the 5 into 3 and 2. So 7 + 5 = 10 + 2 = 12.

items.q: Make ten. 9 + 5 is the same as which?
items.e: Move 1 to make 10. 4 are left. So 9 + 5 = 10 + 4 = 14.

items.q: Make ten. 8 + 4 is the same as which?
items.e: Move 2 to make 10. 2 are left. So 8 + 4 = 10 + 2 = 12.

items.q: Start with the bigger number. What is 4 + 9?
items.e: Start with 9. 9 + 1 = 10. 3 are left. 10 + 3 = 13.

items.q: Start at 8. Count on 3. What is 8 + 3?
items.e: Start at 8. Jump 3 times: 9, 10, 11. You land on 11. (Do not count the 8.)

items.q: Start at 12. Count on 2. What is 12 + 2?
items.e: Start at 12. Jump 2 times: 13, 14. You land on 14. (Do not count the 12.)

items.q: Start at 6. Count on 4. What is 6 + 4?
items.e: Start at 6. Jump 4 times: 7, 8, 9, 10. You land on 10. (Do not count the 6.)

items.q: Start at 15. Count on 3. What is 15 + 3?
items.e: Start at 15. Jump 3 times: 16, 17, 18. You land on 18. (Do not count the 15.)

items.q: Start at 9. Count on 2. What is 9 + 2?
items.e: Start at 9. Jump 2 times: 10, 11. You land on 11. (Do not count the 9.)

items.q: Start at 13. Count on 4. What is 13 + 4?
items.e: Start at 13. Jump 4 times: 14, 15, 16, 17. You land on 17. (Do not count the 13.)

items.q: Start at 11. Count back 3. What is 11 − 3?
items.e: Start at 11. Jump back 3 times: 10, 9, 8. You land on 8. (Do not count the 11.)

items.q: Start at 14. Count back 2. What is 14 − 2?
items.e: Start at 14. Jump back 2 times: 13, 12. You land on 12. (Do not count the 14.)

items.q: Start at 17. Count back 4. What is 17 − 4?
items.e: Start at 17. Jump back 4 times: 16, 15, 14, 13. You land on 13. (Do not count the 17.)

items.q: Start at 9. Count back 3. What is 9 − 3?
items.e: Start at 9. Jump back 3 times: 8, 7, 6. You land on 6. (Do not count the 9.)

items.q: Start at 20. Count back 3. What is 20 − 3?
items.e: Start at 20. Jump back 3 times: 19, 18, 17. You land on 17. (Do not count the 20.)

items.q: Start at 16. Count back 2. What is 16 − 2?
items.e: Start at 16. Jump back 2 times: 15, 14. You land on 14. (Do not count the 16.)

items.q: Which number sentence matches the jumps?
items.e: Start at 7. There are 4 jumps to the right. That is adding: 7 + 4 = 11.

items.q: Which number sentence matches the jumps?
items.e: Start at 15. There are 3 jumps to the left. That is taking away: 15 − 3 = 12.

items.q: Start with the bigger number. What is 2 + 9?
items.e: Start at 9, not 2. Count on 2: 10, 11. So 2 + 9 = 11.

items.q: Start with the bigger number. What is 3 + 12?
items.e: Start at 12, not 3. Count on 3: 13, 14, 15. So 3 + 12 = 15.

items.q: Ethan counts on for 7 + 3. He says “7, 8, 9.” What went wrong?
items.e: Do not say the start number. Start at 7 and say 8, 9, 10. He said 7 too. 7 + 3 = 10.

items.q: Leah counts back for 12 − 2. She says “12, 11.” What went wrong?
items.e: Do not say the start number. Start at 12 and say 11, 10. She said 12 too. 12 − 2 = 10.

items.q: How many jumps from 14 to 18?
items.e: Count the jumps, not the numbers: 15, 16, 17, 18. That is 4 jumps. So 14 + 4 = 18.

items.q: How many jumps back from 19 to 15?
items.e: Count the jumps: 18, 17, 16, 15. That is 4 jumps. So 19 − 4 = 15.

items.q: 8 + 5 = 13. What is 13 − 5?
items.e: Take away the 5 blue counters. 8 red counters are left. 13 − 5 = 8.

items.q: 9 + 3 = 12. What is 12 − 3?
items.e: Take away the 3 blue counters. 9 red counters are left. 12 − 3 = 9.

items.q: 7 + 5 = 12. What is 12 − 5?
items.e: Take away the 5 blue counters. 7 red counters are left. 12 − 5 = 7.

items.q: What is the missing part?
items.e: Think: 8 + ? = 11. 8 + 3 = 11. So the missing part is 3.

items.q: What is the missing part?
items.e: Think: 9 + ? = 14. 9 + 5 = 14. So the missing part is 5.

items.q: What is the missing part?
items.e: Think: 7 + ? = 15. 7 + 8 = 15. So the missing part is 8.

items.q: What is the missing part?
items.e: Think: 4 + ? = 12. 4 + 8 = 12. So the missing part is 8.

items.q: Which addition helps with 15 − 6?
Which addition helps with 11 − 4?
Which fact goes with 9 + 4 = 13?
items.e: A fact family uses the same 3 numbers: 9, 4 and 13. 13 − 4 = 9 uses them.

items.q: 6 + 4 = 10. What is 10 − 4?
items.e: If 6 + 4 = 10, then 10 − 4 = 6. (14 adds instead.)

items.q: Count up from 9 to 12. What is 12 − 9?
items.e: Count up: 10, 11, 12. That is 3 jumps. 9 + 3 = 12. So 12 − 9 = 3.

items.q: Count up from 8 to 16. What is 16 − 8?
Count up from 9 to 17. What is 17 − 9?
Count up from 7 to 13. What is 13 − 7?
Count up from 14 to 20. What is 20 − 14?
Kai says 14 − 5 = 11. What did he do?
items.e: You cannot take 5 from 4, so Kai did 5 − 4 = 1. That is the wrong way. Think: 5 + 9 = 14. So 14 − 5 = 9.

items.q: 15 − 7 = 8. Which addition checks it?
items.e: Add the answer and the number you took away. 8 + 7 = 15. So 15 − 7 = 8 is right.

items.q: 8 + 9 = 17. What is 17 − 9?
items.e: If 8 + 9 = 17, then 17 − 9 = 8. Take away the 9 blue counters.

items.q: 9 + 4 = 13. Which is the turn-around fact?
items.e: A turn-around fact adds the same numbers the other way. The total stays the same: 4 + 9 = 13.

items.q: What is the best way to add 7 + 7?
items.e: 7 + 7 adds a number to itself. Use a double: 7 + 7 = 14.

items.q: What is a good way to add 9 + 6?
items.e: 9 needs just 1 to make 10. Make ten: 9 + 1 = 10, then 10 + 5 = 15.

items.q: What is a good way to add 15 + 2?
items.e: 2 is small. Start at 15 and count on 2: 16, 17. So 15 + 2 = 17.

items.q: What is a good way to find 13 − 9?
items.e: 9 and 13 are close. Think 9 + ? = 13. Count up: 10, 11, 12, 13. That is 4.

items.q: Liam has 6 hockey pucks. He gets 6 more. How many pucks now?
items.e: This is a double. 6 + 6 = 12.

items.q: 9 students are on the bus. 4 more get on. How many now?
items.e: Make ten. 9 + 1 = 10. 3 more is 13.

items.q: Emma picks 7 apples. Noah picks 8 apples. How many apples?
items.e: Near double. Double 7 is 14. 1 more is 15.

items.q: 12 Canada geese are on the pond. 3 fly away. How many are left?
items.e: Count back 3: 11, 10, 9. So 9 are left.

items.q: 14 students skate at the rink. 5 go home. How many still skate?
items.e: 14 − 4 = 10. Take away 1 more: 9. Check: 9 + 5 = 14.

items.q: Maya reads 8 pages on Monday. She reads 8 on Tuesday. How many pages?
items.e: This is a double. 8 + 8 = 16.

items.q: Ava has 15 hockey cards. Kai has 9. How many more does Ava have?
items.e: Count up from 9 to 15: 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15. That is 6.

items.q: The bus has 20 seats. 14 students sit down. How many seats are empty?
items.e: Think: 14 + ? = 20. 14 + 6 = 20. So 6 seats are empty.

items.q: Some loons swim on the lake. 5 more come. Now there are 13. How many were there at first?
items.e: Think: ? + 5 = 13. 8 + 5 = 13. So there were 8 loons.

items.q: Zoe has 7 stickers. She gets some more. Now she has 12. How many did she get?
items.e: Count up from 7 to 12: 8, 9, 10, 11, 12. That is 5. Check: 7 + 5 = 12.

items.q: 10 pairs of mitts are in the lost and found. 4 pairs go home. How many pairs are left?
Mateo picks 18 maple leaves. He gives 9 to Hana. How many does he have now?
items.e: Double 9 is 18. So 18 − 9 = 9. Check: 9 + 9 = 18.

items.q: Sofia puts 5 red, 5 blue and 4 green beads on a string. How many beads?
11 students play in the snow at recess. 3 go inside. Then 5 come out. How many are outside now?
items.e: Step 1: 11 − 3 = 8. Step 2: 8 + 5 = 13. (8 stops after step 1.)

items.q: Arjun says 9 + 5 = 14. Which fact checks it?
items.e: Take one part away from the whole. 14 − 5 = 9, so Arjun is right.

items.q: Priya says 16 − 7 = 8. Is she right?
items.e: Check with addition: 8 + 7 = 15, not 16. Count up from 7 to 16: that is 9. No. It is 9.
